title.narrative: Provision of technical support to nutrition partners responding to eastern DRC crisis to strengthen nutrition coordination, needs assessment and analysis, and response

description.narrative: NiE stakeholders in the DRC, especially local and national nutrition actors, have increased capacities and access to tools and guidance to respond to the nutrition crises in North Kivu and South Kivu Provinces, thereby improving the coverage and quality of the emergency response.

This project will strengthen the effectiveness and quality of the nutrition response in South Kivu and North Kivu provinces by providing technical expertise to the Nutrition Cluster, including local and national actors, who are responding to the current crisis. This project will provide technical support services in three areas that were identified as high priority by the DRC Nutrition Cluster and PRONANUT (Ministry of Health) – co -lead of the Nutrition Cluster.

title.narrative: As per initial project proposal the overarching aim of this project was that: NiE stakeholders in the DRC, especially local and national nutrition actors, have increased capacities and access to tools and guidance to respond to the nutrition crises in North Kivu and South Kivu Provinces, thereby improving the coverage and quality of the emergency response.

description.narrative:
This aim was met with the implementation of cluster coordination, information management, NIS and NiE support, totalling 50 weeks of technical assistance.
Nutrition response quality and effectiveness has been, and will continue to be, improved with the appropriate implementation of the minimum NiE package, the PRONUTUR and the nutrition surveillance decision tree, which will improve the coherence, replicability and coordination of emergency responses going forward. Increased capacities in adaptations to wasting management will mean more children can be reached with quality wasting treatment (see qualitative feedback in section 2.3), which has been adapted for the emergency context in eastern DRC. More children will also be reached thanks to increased capacities to do rapid SMART/CDC MUAC screenings, which is a simpler and more effective tool for conducting screenings than previous methodologies. Coherence and accountability have been improved with increased capacities in cluster coordination and specific governance documents to structure humanitarian coordination activities (e.g. cluster ToRs). In addition, the improvements made to the cluster dashboard and bulletin mean that it is easier to monitor the nutrition response and account for activities and achievements in a transparent manner. By integrating community data into the SNSAP, the DRC nutrition cluster will also be able to generate hot spot analysis in a more effective way, giving a fuller picture of sentinel site data. This is particularly important in a context of data scarcity and reduced funding for full-scale nutrition assessments (e.g. SMART surveys). The updated nutrition sector severity analysis tool also allows for a more transparent prioritisation process and greater accountability with regards to allocating resources.
As per feedback that was formally shared by the DRC Nutrition Cluster Coordinator4, the technical support provided by this project: “[…] contributed significantly to strengthening national capacities. There was a clear transfer of skills through co-facilitation, joint development of tools, and participatory methodologies that the local team can now replicate independently. The exercise also led to the setup and consolidation of new systems such as the structured minimum package for NiE and the integrated activation/deactivation criteria for simplified approaches. Additionally, the updated training package and the facilitation techniques introduced (interactive tools, scenario-based learning) have improved the cluster’s training standards and partner engagement practices.”
When responding to the GNC Operations Team’s 3-month post support survey (NiE assignment), the DRC Nutrition Cluster Coordinator also responded “agree” to the following statement ”GNC support led to improved quality of nutrition emergency preparedness, response or recovery”. Additional post-support survey data for cluster coordination, IM and NIS assignments is not available at the time of writing the report (given these assignments have only just wrapped up) but will be available from April 2026 onwards.
In addition to its 3-month post deployment survey, the GNC Operations team also developed a specific survey to ascertain the uptake of the NiE minimum package and the training on adaptations to wasting management. These are highlighted below. Though the response rate was low (only 10 respondents) they do highlight a trend of using, or partially using, the knowledge and resources provided within current nutrition programming.

title.narrative: 1 PRONUTUR developed for three provinces (North Kivu, South Kivu and Ituri) and validated by the Goma and Bunia sub-national nutrition clusters, the ProNaNut and cluster partners
12 people (17% women, 83% men) trained on cluster coordination, of which 17% were local or national partners
67 people trained on CDC/SMART rapid MUAC screening tool.
Combined North and South Kivu sub-national cluster (based in Goma) and Ituri sub-national cluster (based in Bunia) have been strengthened and are fully functional
Nutrition assessment decision tree developed and cluster prioritisation tool updated
Nutrition information management dashboard developed and maintained with up-to-date information on the evolution of the response
Sentinel site integration strategy technical developed, along with associated community reporting format
Technical note for adaptations to wasting management developed and disseminated
